subject: Ropers et al. (2011)
object: Ropers et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID), which they described as non-syndromic.

subject: Ropers et al. (2011)
object: In a large consanguineous family with ARID, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, together with targeted exon enrichment and high-throughput sequencing, to identify the underlying gene defect.

subject: Ropers et al. (2011)
object: In affected members of a large consanguineous family with ARID, Ropers et al. (2011) found a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP gene, a member of the WASH complex. After SNP filtering, it was one of only two remaining changes. The authors considered it causative based on high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores and on functional considerations. Functional studies showed that the mutation significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex.

subject: WASHC4 non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP gene
Ropers et al. (2011)
object: Ropers et al. (2011) noted that SWIP belongs to the WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and in multiple endosomal transport processes. They suggested that SWIP is a novel gene for ARID, because the mutation destabilized the WASH complex.

subject: Assoum et al. (2020)
object: Assoum et al. (2020) described 2 sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, with syndromic intellectual disability. Both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

subject: Assoum et al. (2020)
object: In 2 sisters with syndromic intellectual disability, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous variants in the KIAA1033 (WASHC4) gene by exome sequencing: a stop-gain variant (p.Gln442Ter) and a missense variant (p.Asp1048Gly), each inherited from one parent.

subject: Assoum et al. (2020)
object: Assoum et al. (2020) described a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly.

subject: Assoum et al. (2020)
object: In a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous missense variants in the KIAA1033 gene, p.Lys1079Arg and p.His503Arg, one inherited from each parent, by exome sequencing.

subject: Assoum et al. (2020)
object: Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that KIAA1033 is responsible for a heterogeneous autosomal recessive intellectual disability phenotype and that further descriptions would be needed to refine the clinical phenotype.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from 7 children with homozygous WASHC4 c.3056C>G mutations originally reported by Ropers et al. (2011), who had been evaluated at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman. Although developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary reason for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms at a mean age of 10.4 years, with movements described as 'clumsy' and with fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) reported that recent communication with the parents of the WASHC4 c.3056C>G homozygous patients, who were by then an average of 21 years old, revealed no notable exacerbation of symptoms; the authors suggested that the SWIPP1019R mouse model either differs from human patients or may predict future disease progression in these individuals, since mice worsened significantly at 5-6 months of age (thought to be equivalent to ~30-35 human years).

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) studied the autosomal recessive WASHC4 mutation c.3056C>G (p.Pro1019Arg), previously identified by Ropers et al. (2011) in a cohort of children with nonsyndromic intellectual disability, noting that the affected residue lies in a region of SWIP thought to be critical for binding the WASH component Strumpellin. Co-immunoprecipitation in HEK cells showed that mutant SWIP pulled down significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wild-type SWIP (54.8% and 41.4% of wild type, respectively), indicating that the mutation hinders WASH complex formation.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) proposed that WASH complex destabilization resulting from SWIPP1019R drives cognitive and motor impairments via endo-lysosomal dysfunction in the brain, with accumulation of neurodegenerative markers including upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin build-up, and cleaved caspase-3 over time.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) generated a CRISPR knock-in mouse carrying a CCT>CGT point mutation in exon 29 of murine Washc4, mimicking the human WASHC4 c.3056C>G (SWIPP1019R) variant. Western blotting of adult whole-brain lysate from homozygous mutant mice showed near-complete loss of the WASH complex members Strumpellin (3.8% of wild type) and WASH1 (1.1% of wild type), phenocopying data from the human patients and indicating WASH complex instability in vivo.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) found by tandem-mass-tag spatial proteomics of 10-month-old SWIPP1019R mutant mouse brain that four WASH proteins (WASHC1, WASHC2, WASHC4, WASHC5) and RAB21A were differentially abundant in all seven subcellular fractions, that 728 proteins differed overall between genotypes, and that a WASH/CCC/Retriever/CORVET-HOPS-containing endosomal module (M38) was significantly decreased while a lysosomal module (M36) containing cathepsins, hydrolases and progranulin was significantly increased in mutant brain.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) showed that cultured cortical neurons from SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice had enlarged somatic EEA1+ early endosomes without a change in puncta number, and fewer but larger Cathepsin D+ lysosomal puncta than wild-type neurons, consistent with a loss-of-function mutation producing morphological abnormalities of the endo-lysosomal pathway.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) found that 10-month-old SWIPP1019R mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining in motor cortex (44.0% vs 25.4% of DAPI+ nuclei) but not at adolescence, and that transmission electron microscopy of 7-month-old mutant motor cortex revealed large electron-dense lipofuscin deposits; dopaminergic cell number in substantia nigra pars compacta and striatal dopaminergic innervation were unchanged, suggesting motor cortex was the primary movement-related region altered.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) reported that SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice performed normally in novel object recognition and Y-maze alternation but showed a significant deficit in cued fear memory recall 48 hours after tone-footshock pairing at both adolescence (P42) and adulthood (6.5 months), with intact responses to footshock and tones, consistent with the hypothesis that SWIPP1019R causes cognitive impairment in humans.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) found that SWIPP1019R homozygous mutant mice showed an almost 50% reduction in rotarod retention time at both P45 and 5.5 months, and that TreadScan gait analysis, largely normal at adolescence, revealed by 5.5 months significantly longer hindlimb swing times, longer stride lengths, and decreased homologous coupling, demonstrating progressive motor decline.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) used in vivo BioID with a WASH1-BioID2 probe expressed under the human synapsin-1 promoter in mouse brain to define the neuronal WASH complex proteome, identifying 175 significantly enriched proteins (fold-change >=4, FDR <0.05) that included all five WASH complex subunits and 13 previously reported WASH interactors, as well as endosomal, endocytic, cytoskeletal and excitatory postsynaptic proteins, supporting a major endosomal trafficking role for WASH in mouse brain.

subject: Courtland et al. (2021)
object: Courtland et al. (2021) noted that dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8), and that autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and nonsyndromic intellectual disabilities.

subject: Gangfuß et al. (2022)
object: Gangfuß et al. (2022) reported 2 sisters with a syndromic phenotype that included dysmorphic features, intellectual disability, profound developmental disorder, and skeletal muscle involvement. The authors said these features expanded the clinical spectrum of WASHC4-related disease, and they compared the phenotype with previously reported cases.

subject: Gangfuß et al. (2022)
object: In 2 sisters with intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and skeletal muscle involvement, Gangfuß et al. (2022) identified a homozygous variant in the WASHC4 gene. The abstract does not give the specific variant.

subject: Gangfuß et al. (2022)
object: Gangfuß et al. (2022) found that proteomic profiling of fibroblasts from a WASHC4-deficient patient showed dysregulation of proteins relevant for maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Immunostaining of the same patient's muscle biopsy confirmed dysregulation of proteins needed for proper muscle function. The authors said histologic studies and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopy supported a role for WASHC4 in protein processing and clearance in humans.
